analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal strings on drinking water systems and eases infrastructure loan repayment terms.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and never received a committee hearing or vote; it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite parts of the Safe Drinking Water Act. It would let water systems repay federal infrastructure loans over longer periods — up to 40 years for disadvantaged communities — and would raise the share of loan money states may forgive for poor communities from 30% to 35% [S2, S3]. It would also strip a rule that requires the EPA to keep drinking water standards at least as protective of health when it updates them, and would exempt water projects funded with federal loans from federal requirements whenever a state rule is judged just as strict [S2, S3]. In addition, it would remove the requirement that states put up matching funds for federal drinking water loans and direct federal money toward protecting sources of drinking water through 2024 [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Households in disadvantaged communities that struggle to pay water bills would benefit from longer loan repayment terms and a larger share of forgiven loan money, which can lower the rates that fund water system upgrades [S2, S3]. Public water systems — mostly municipal utilities — would get cheaper, longer-term financing and fewer federal requirements attached to federally funded projects [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Poor communities facing high water bills

how_it_helps.text: Extends loan repayment to 30 years, and up to 40 years for disadvantaged communities, so water system upgrades can be paid off over more time and financed with smaller rate increases [S3].
Raises the maximum additional loan subsidy states must make available to disadvantaged communities from 30% to 35% of funds [S3].

Exempts federally funded water projects from federal cross-cutting requirements when a state or local rule is considered equally strict, reducing paperwork and compliance costs for water systems [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Future revisions of national drinking water standards could be less protective of health, because the bill removes the requirement that EPA maintain or improve protection when updating rules [S2, S3]. Workers on federally funded water projects could lose federal job-site protections, such as wage standards, whenever a state rule is deemed equivalent [S3]. Federal taxpayers would bear more of the cost of water loans, since states would no longer be required to match federal drinking water funds [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes the Safe Drinking Water Act's requirement that EPA maintain or provide greater health protection when revising national drinking water regulations, opening the door to weaker standards in future updates [S2, S3].

Once the EPA determines a state rule is as strict as a federal cross-cutting requirement, the bill says the agency 'shall exempt' funded projects from the federal requirement — meaning federal worker- and project-protection conditions on loans could be waived with limited review [S3].
Removing the state matching-fund requirement means federal drinking water loans would flow without states putting up their own money, shifting more of the cost to federal taxpayers [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The affordability provisions are real: longer loan terms and a larger forgiveness share for disadvantaged communities would ease the burden of financing water system repairs, which falls on ratepayers, many of them in low-income communities. But those gains are bought partly by weakening two federal safeguards — the floor on how protective drinking water standards must stay, and federal conditions attached to federal infrastructure money. Whether that trade is worth it depends on trusting states to replicate federal protections; the bill makes the exemption mandatory once EPA makes that judgment, which reduces oversight.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and sat there until the 114th Congress ended, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta (R-OH) introduced the Drinking Water Affordability Act of 2016 on December 1, 2016 [S1, S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, where all further action would have had to begin [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; with the 114th Congress ending on January 3, 2017, the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing requirement that EPA keep drinking water standards at least as protective when updating them, and federal conditions attached to infrastructure loans, stayed in place. At the same time, communities struggling with water bills got none of the loan relief the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal drinking water safeguards; no bill relief

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to committee; no cosponsors joined.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; its only sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Public water systems and municipal utilities
industries.note: The bill gives water systems longer, cheaper federal financing and exempts funded projects from federal requirements when state rules are judged equivalent, lowering the compliance costs that flow into customer rates. But the same relaxation could allow weaker drinking water standards over time, a cost borne by the people the systems serve.

Longer loan terms and expanded lending would support more water projects, more work for contractors. The exemption from federal cross-cutting requirements could strip federal conditions such as prevailing-wage rules from those projects, cutting costs for contractors while reducing protections for construction workers.
